This sets off so many alarm bells for me.

Justin Kao heard about the discovery of a “sweet tooth gene” that makes you more likely to crave sweets. “Oh my God,” thought Kao, who has always loved cookies. “I would pay $5 to know if I had that.”

Kao is hoping that millions of other people will be just as eager to spend a few bucks for tidbits revealed in their DNA.

Now we will have micro-transactions for medical diagnosis.

Helix’s idea is to collect a spit sample from anyone who buys a DNA app, sequence and analyze the customers’ genes, and then digitize the findings so they can be accessed by software developers who want to sell other apps. Helix calls the idea “sequence once, query often.” (The company says customers will find these apps on websites and possibly in the Android and Apple app stores.)

Potentially huge, private database of individual's DNA. This will be accessible by individuals/organizations not bound by doctor-patient confidentiality over a medium (mobile/web) easily compromised.

Customers will control their data by deciding who sees it. There’s even a “nuclear button” to erase every A, G, C, and T. But key details are still being sorted out.Will people be able to download their DNA information and take it elsewhere? Probably, though they might pay extra for the privilege.

Here they try and reassure people on the risks while not explicitly saying whether the company retains rights to the data collected and what they can do (read sell) with it. If you pay for the privilege that means they control the rights is how I read that.

DNA sequencing could be revolutionary for preventative care but this avenue seems very perilous.
